method: Each bucket classifies a common AI-work request as SOLVED-NOW (a shipping product already does it), DIY-WITH-GUIDE (no engineer required), or NEEDS-A-HUMAN (genuinely custom). Prices are quoted from the sources listed on each bucket and go stale; the as_of date says when each verdict was made and the flip field says what would change it.

buckets.title: Notes, summaries and action items from meetings
buckets.answer: Nothing to build here. Every major meeting platform ships this now, and several standalone tools have free tiers that cover an individual's whole usage.
buckets.detail: Built-in options are Zoom AI Companion, Google Meet's 'take notes for me' (Gemini) and Microsoft Copilot's Intelligent Recap — invisible to other participants and needing no setup, but platform-locked and often tied to a higher subscription tier. Standalone tools work across platforms.

buckets.title: Asking questions across your own documents
buckets.answer: Source-grounded document Q&A is a free consumer feature. Commissioning a retrieval pipeline for this is one of the most common pieces of avoidable AI spend.
buckets.detail: The distinction that matters: a source-grounded tool answers only from the documents you gave it and cites the exact passage, which is what you want for policies and contracts. A general assistant is more flexible but more likely to drift from your files.

tools.name: NotebookLM / Gemini Notebook
tools.note: 100 notebooks, 50 sources each, 50 chat queries/day; answers cite the passage. Renamed Gemini Notebook on 2026-07-16 — same tool, same limits

buckets.flip: The free query limits fall below everyday use, or source-grounded citation is removed — at which point a paid tool, still not a build, is the answer.

buckets.title: A chatbot answering customers on your website
buckets.answer: This is a product you configure, not a system you build. The decision that actually costs you money is the billing model, not the vendor.
buckets.detail: Per-resolution billing looks cheap at pilot volume and scales badly; flat plans often cost less once you are busy. Price the vendor at the volume you expect in a year, not the volume you have this month.

tools.name: Tidio (Lyro AI)
tools.price: Lyro add-on $39/mo for 50 conversations up to $289/mo for 500

tools.name: Intercom (Fin)
tools.price: $0.99 per resolution plus seats at $29/$85/$132 per seat/mo
tools.note: 50-resolution monthly minimum; at 2,000 resolutions/month that is $1,980/mo in AI fees alone

buckets.flip: Any of these vendors changes billing model, or your volume passes the point where a per-resolution plan beats a flat one — recheck the arithmetic, not the vendor list.

buckets.title: Making two apps talk, with an AI step in the middle
buckets.answer: This is the single most common thing sold as 'an AI agent'. It is a workflow in an automation tool, there is probably a published template for it, and you can build it in an afternoon.
buckets.detail: The billing models differ in ways that decide the cost: Zapier charges per step, Make per module, n8n per workflow run. At 5,000–20,000 tasks a month Zapier typically runs $49–299/mo while Make runs $16–29/mo for equivalent work — so a multi-step workflow is where Zapier gets expensive.
steps: Write the sentence 'when X happens in app A, do Y in app B' — if you cannot, the problem is not automation yet.
Search your automation tool's template gallery for that exact pair before building anything.
Add at most one AI step, and only where the input is genuinely unstructured text.
Run it in manual-approve mode for a week. Anything that surprises you now would have surprised you in production.
Only then turn it on unattended — and set a failure notification, because silent failure is the real cost.

tools.note: per-workflow-run billing; self-hosting is genuinely free if you can run a container

buckets.title: Sorting, labelling or routing incoming email
buckets.answer: Rules first, AI second. Most of this is a mail filter, and the part that genuinely needs a model is one step inside an automation tool.
buckets.detail: The reason to do rules first is not purity, it is debugging: when a deterministic filter misroutes something you can see why, and when a model does you often cannot. Use the model only for the part that is actually unstructured — pulling a reference number out of free text, or classifying tone.
steps: Write down the five categories you actually want. If you cannot name them, no system can sort into them.
Build whatever you can as plain mail rules — sender, subject, keyword. This handles more than people expect.
For the genuinely unstructured part, add one AI step in an automation tool that extracts the field you need.
Send low-confidence cases to a review folder rather than guessing. A wrong file is worse than an unfiled one.
Check the review folder weekly — that is your measurement of whether it is working.

route.label: Rather someone else built it? See n8n's partner directory
route.disclosure: Zapier's equivalent is zapier.com/partnerdirectory. Neither is vetted by this site — but a tool vendor's own directory is narrower and higher-intent than a general marketplace for a job this specific.

buckets.flip: Mailbox providers ship reliable AI-native rules built in, which would move this to SOLVED-NOW.

buckets.title: What it should cost, and how to vet who is quoting you
buckets.answer: Two answers in one: what this work actually costs, and the four questions that tell you whether the person quoting is real.
buckets.detail: Published rates disagree, and the disagreement is the useful part: Upwork's own AI-agent-developer category page cites $30–150/hr, specialist rate cards put freelance AI agent developers at $155–185/hr, and broader surveys give $80–250/hr globally — roughly $50–80 junior, $80–120 mid, $120–200 senior, with LLM specialisation adding a 30–50% premium and regulated domains 20–40%. Marketplace fees come out of what your builder receives, so they shape the quote: Upwork moved to a variable 0–15% per-contract freelancer fee on 2025-05-01 (most pay around 10%), and Fiverr takes a flat 20%. A quote outside those bands is not automatically wrong — it needs an explanation. And Gartner predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027.
buckets.typical_cost: $30–150/hr per Upwork's own category page; $155–185/hr per specialist rate cards; $80–250/hr across broader surveys ($50–80 junior, $80–120 mid, $120–200 senior). Before comparing a fixed-price quote, divide it by the hours it implies and see which band it lands in.
steps: Ask what the system does when the model is wrong. A real builder has a specific answer with a fallback path; agent-washing has a reassurance.
Ask for a live demo on your data, not their demo data. The gap between the two is where most projects die.
Ask which parts are deterministic code and which are model calls. If everything is 'the AI', nobody has designed it.
Ask what one run costs at your volume, in dollars, at the volume you will have in a year — not today's pilot volume.
Ask what you own at the end and whether it runs without them. If the answer is unclear, that is the price of the second project too.
buckets.flip: Gartner publishes a materially different vendor-reality estimate, the cancellation prediction resolves (its own horizon is end of 2027), or the rate bands move enough that a quote inside them stops being a useful signal.

buckets.title: An agent that has to drive your internal or legacy system
buckets.answer: This is genuinely custom. No product knows your internal system, and the work is mostly the integration and the failure handling, not the model.
buckets.detail: Be aware of what you are actually buying: in most of these projects the AI is a small part and the integration is the project. Price it as an integration job with an AI step, and be suspicious of anyone who prices it the other way round.
ask_for: Which exact system and version, and whether it has any API, export, or database access at all — this single answer moves the price more than anything else.
What happens when the agent is wrong or the system is down: the specific fallback, not a promise of accuracy.
Which parts will be deterministic code and which will be model calls.
Who holds the credentials during and after the build, and how they are rotated at handover.
What you own at the end, and a demonstration that it runs without the builder.
The running cost per month at your real volume, itemised — model calls, hosting, and their retainer separately.
buckets.typical_cost: Rate sources disagree, and the gap is worth knowing: Upwork's own AI-agent-developer page cites $30–150/hr, while specialist rate cards put freelance AI agent developers at $155–185/hr; broader surveys give $80–250/hr globally, roughly $50–80 junior, $80–120 mid, $120–200 senior. Treat a quote outside those bands as needing an explanation, not as automatically wrong.
buckets.red_flag: They quote a fixed price before asking which system you run, or they call a scripted integration an 'AI agent'.

buckets.title: An AI feature inside a product you already ship
buckets.answer: Hire for this, but hire for evaluation as much as for building. Shipping a model into a product your customers already trust is a quality-control problem wearing an engineering costume.
buckets.detail: The demo is the easy part and takes days. What takes months is knowing whether it is still working next quarter, on inputs nobody anticipated. If a proposal has no evaluation plan, it is a prototype quote priced as a product.
ask_for: How we will know it works: the evaluation set, who writes it, and what score is the ship threshold.
The latency and cost budget per request, and what happens when a request exceeds it.
The behaviour on a bad or unsafe output — visible to the user, or caught first, and by what.
How a regression is detected after launch, given the model provider can change under you.
Whether the design survives switching model providers, and what that migration would cost.
What is logged, where it is stored, and how that squares with what you have told your customers.
buckets.typical_cost: Same rate bands as custom agent work — Upwork's category page cites $30–150/hr, specialist rate cards $155–185/hr, broader surveys $80–250/hr — but expect evaluation and monitoring to be a real line item rather than a rounding error. A proposal with no such line is the thing to question.
buckets.red_flag: No evaluation plan, or a fixed price for 'AI integration' with no mention of what happens when the output is wrong.

buckets.title: An agent that spends money, sends things, or changes records
buckets.answer: Hire, and hire specifically for the failure design. The model is not the hard part; the hard part is what the system is permitted to do when it is confidently wrong.
buckets.detail: Gartner's stated reasons for the cancellation rate are escalating costs, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. This bucket is where the third reason bites, because the mistakes are not recoverable by re-running the job.
ask_for: The blast radius: the maximum damage one wrong action can do, stated in money or records.
Which actions require a human approval step, and why the others do not.
The rate limits and hard caps, and where they are enforced — in the agent's own reasoning does not count.
How an action is reversed, and who is paged when one cannot be.
The audit trail: what is recorded for every action, and can you read it without the builder.
A dry-run mode you can leave on for a month before anything is live.
buckets.typical_cost: Same rate bands as custom agent work, but budget separately for the review period — the cost of this category is dominated by the supervised run-in, not the build.
buckets.red_flag: Approval steps are described as a temporary phase to remove later, or the caps live inside the prompt rather than in the code around it.

buckets.title: An AI that answers or makes phone calls
buckets.answer: There are products in this space, but the deployment is not self-serve: telephony, recording consent and call-handling rules are jurisdiction-specific, and getting them wrong is a legal problem rather than a quality one.
buckets.detail: Treat the recording and disclosure rules as the first question rather than a detail at the end — they differ by country and by state, and they determine what the system is allowed to do before any vendor comparison matters.
ask_for: Which jurisdictions your callers are in, and what each requires for recording and AI disclosure.
What the system says when someone asks whether they are talking to a machine.
The handoff to a human: how it is triggered, how fast, and what happens outside working hours.
Per-minute running cost at your real call volume, including the telephony leg.
What is retained from each call, for how long, and where.
buckets.typical_cost: Not published here — we have not verified a current rate range specific to voice agent work, and the rate cards we did verify cover agent development generally rather than telephony deployments. Ask for a fixed scope quote and compare at least three.
buckets.red_flag: Recording consent and AI disclosure are treated as a footnote, or the quote covers the agent but not the telephony bill.
